tldr: Standard PX4 firmware and QGroundControl were extended for hybrid unmanned aerial-aquatic vehicles (UAAVs) that combine flying drone and surface boat capabilities, enabling end-to-end autonomous execution of flight, landing on water, surface navigation, and takeoff within a single system.
hero_caption: State diagram of the proposed PX4 extension architecture. (a) shows the marine navigation management module controlling manual/autonomous switching and safety interventions, and (b) shows the Navigator module autonomously handling transitions from waypoint altitude evaluation to landing, water surface navigation, and takeoff back to a safe altitude.
overview:
Surveying aquatic environments such as oceans and lakes comes with substantial costs and operational risks, including arranging boats and divers, as well as mitigating noise and pollution. Hybrid unmanned aerial-aquatic vehicles (UAAVs) have attracted attention as a solution, moving rapidly through the air and landing on the water surface as needed to perform sampling and close-up observation.

However, major open-source autopilots like PX4 and ArduPilot have fundamentally been developed as separate systems for aerial and marine domains. Because of this, it was difficult to plan and execute a hybrid mission—where a single vehicle flies through the air, alights on the water to navigate, and takes off again to return—seamlessly using a single firmware and ground control station (GCS).

In this study, the authors developed custom PX4 firmware that integrates a marine navigation module and autonomous mission transition logic while preserving PX4's standard architecture and safety mechanisms. Ground control software QGroundControl (QGC) was also extended so flight paths and water-surface paths can be distinguished automatically based solely on waypoint altitude settings.

For validation, Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) simulations were performed using Gazebo Garden and Virtual RobotX (VRX). Stable tracking of a boustrophedon (lawnmower) path was confirmed not only on calm water but also in a wavy environment with a 1.5 m wave height, handling wave disturbances and turning delays.
contributions: Natively integrated dedicated marine navigation modules without disrupting PX4's modular architecture or safety mechanisms
Extended Navigator to automatically switch between flight, landing, surface navigation, and takeoff based on waypoint altitude checks
Implemented manual virtual-rudder control and path-following control laws with disturbance compensation inside PX4 for an underactuated two-thruster configuration
Enhanced usability in QGroundControl by introducing color-coded marine/aerial waypoints and direct selection of the new navigation modes

sections.heading: Why integrate the 'brain' of a hybrid aerial-marine drone?
sections.summary: To cut surveying costs and safety risks in aquatic environments, hybrid drones combining flight and surface navigation are drawing high expectations. However, existing open-source autopilots focus on a single domain, leaving no unified control system for both environments.
sections.details:
Mapping and environmental monitoring in aquatic environments are extremely costly, requiring skilled crews, dedicated vessels, and extensive logistics. Operational vessel noise and water pollution also raise concerns about harmful impacts on surveyed ecosystems. These issues drive the search for robotic surveying methods that reduce manpower and environmental footprint.

Hybrid unmanned aerial-aquatic vehicles (UAAVs) are especially promising platforms, handling wide-area aerial exploration alongside surface landing for close-range measurement and water sampling in one vehicle. Yet widely used autopilot software suites—such as PX4, ArduPilot, and iNav—remain split into separate configurations for drones and unmanned surface vehicles (USVs). They have lacked the capability to integrate aerial flight and water-surface navigation into a single control and mission execution architecture.

To address this gap, this paper proposes custom firmware that natively integrates marine navigation modes and mission management mechanisms while maintaining PX4's modular structure and safety features. PX4 was selected as the base platform due to its permissive BSD license, and the entire developed codebase has been released as open-source software to the community.

sections.heading: Trends in aerial-aquatic robotics and the firmware integration challenge
sections.summary: While research has explored multi-vehicle UAV-USV coordination and fixed-wing hybrid craft, almost no studies have achieved autonomous transitions and surface propulsion control inside a single autopilot for multicopter-style UAAVs. This work is a pioneering effort achieving integration at the PX4 firmware level.
sections.details:
In marine exploration, many studies report combining aerial drones (UAVs) for rapid wide-area aerial imaging with surface vessels (USVs) or underwater vehicles (UUVs) for persistent surface data collection. For example, cooperative inspection systems using UAVs, USVs, and UUVs together to inspect floating structures have been proposed.

Practical applications of open-source ArduPilot-based USVs for water quality sampling have also advanced, demonstrating that robotics effectively cuts costs and improves data quality. However, most prior work relied either on cooperative multi-robot teams or, in single-vehicle cases, on two separate onboard flight controllers switched between flight and water modes. One example controlling air and water on a single PX4 base is the sailing fixed-wing platform "SailMAV", but that was a specialized design tailored specifically to wind-powered sailing.

### Novelty and contributions of this work
In short, no prior multicopter-type UAAV with active thruster propulsion has integrated flight, landing, surface navigation, takeoff, and ground-station interfacing inside a single firmware package. To fill this gap, this research significantly extends PX4's navigation pipeline and QGroundControl to realize a unified hybrid mission environment.

sections.heading: Embedding marine navigation and autonomous mission transitions into the core of PX4
sections.summary: Following PX4's modular design, the authors implemented a 50 Hz Marine Navigation module alongside a custom Navigator module that manages flight, landing, surface navigation, and takeoff via waypoint altitude thresholds. Integration with QGroundControl enables color-coded marine waypoints and direct selection of the new modes.
sections.details:
The proposed system adheres to PX4's native modular architecture, safely exchanging data with the existing flight control pipeline through uORB topics.

### 3.1 Marine Navigation module
This core component manages all surface behavior. It inherits from PX4 standard base classes (ModuleBase, ModuleParams, ScheduledWorkItem) and runs as a ScheduledWorkItem at 50 Hz. The module oversees two modes: Manual Navigation and Autonomous Navigation. Modes transition from an idle state via uORB messages, and a failsafe ensures operators can take manual control (either aerial or marine) at any time via an RC safety switch even during autonomous navigation.

### 3.2 Navigator module extensions
Branching logic for surface phases was added to PX4's Navigator module (such as mission.cpp and mission_base.cpp), which oversees mission execution. It checks the altitude of each waypoint set in QGC and automatically categorizes points below a user-defined threshold as "marine waypoints". When a marine waypoint is detected during flight, the vehicle first approaches directly above it, aligns its heading toward the subsequent marine target, and performs a Landing. Once landing is complete, aerial controls are bypassed, autonomous surface navigation begins, and if the next waypoint at the end of the marine route is aerial, the vehicle automatically initiates a Takeoff to a safe altitude before resuming standard flight mission logic.

### 3.3 QGroundControl (QGC) extensions
Intuitive UI enhancements were applied to the ground station. Synchronizing with PX4's nav_state enables "PRISMA Auto Marine" and "PRISMA Manual TS" to appear directly in the flight mode selection menu. Furthermore, in the mission planning screen, waypoints evaluated as marine points are automatically highlighted in blue, allowing operators to distinguish flight segments from water segments at a glance.

sections.heading: Propelling the vehicle on water: control allocation and tracking logic with disturbance compensation
sections.summary: For a UAAV model equipped with twin pontoon floats and two fixed thrusters, the authors developed manual virtual-rudder control and an autonomous path-following control law based on input-output feedback linearization. Combining a forward hand-position control point with online current disturbance estimation achieves accurate path following during turns and under ambient drift.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Vehicle specifications and low-speed kinematic model
The target UAAV features two buoyant pontoons mounted beneath a quadcopter frame, along with two fixed electric thrusters on the left and right sides. Low-speed surface navigation dynamics are described by a 3-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) model spanning surge ($x$), sway ($y$), and yaw (rotation $\psi$).

### 4.2 Control allocation
The general thrust allocation model for vectored-thruster vessels is reduced to fit this vehicle's two fixed thrusters. Given left and right thruster forces $T_{\mathrm{L}}, T_{\mathrm{R}}$, the resulting surge force $f_x$ and yaw moment $n$ are uniquely mapped to PWM signals through a straightforward geometric transformation matrix based on thruster separation.

### 4.3 Manual navigation control: intuitive virtual rudder
In manual mode, RC throttle and roll stick inputs are read as total thrust $t \in [-1, 1]$ and steering angle $s \in [-1, 1]$. Using a feedforward control structure where thrust commands are $T_{\mathrm{L}} = t + s$ and $T_{\mathrm{R}} = t - s$ (normalized if magnitudes exceed 1), operators enjoy an intuitive, responsive steering feel, including pivot turns on the spot without forward speed.

### 4.4 Autonomous navigation control: hand-position method and current compensation
A twin-thruster hull lacks lateral propulsion, forming an underactuated system. The authors adopt an approach that defines a virtual control point $h$ (hand-position point) placed a forward distance $l$ ahead of the center of mass. Because surge thrust and yaw moment at the center of mass completely control the 2D acceleration of point $h$, input-output feedback linearization becomes applicable.

Target paths consist of straight-line segments, and path progression $\dot{s}$ is automatically slowed down according to the tracking error $e_h$ via $\dot{s} = \dot{s}_{\mathrm{nom}}(1 - \tanh(e_h^2))$. This prevents the virtual target point from pulling ahead during turns and causing error divergence. Furthermore, water current component $\hat{v}_c$ is estimated online from ground velocity (via GNSS and IMU) and hand-point velocity errors, cancelling steady-state disturbances alongside an integrator. To avoid learning errors during turning transients, a gating mechanism updates disturbance estimates only when the vehicle's ground velocity vector is sufficiently aligned with the path tangent ($g_{\mathrm{align,th}} \ge 0.75$ and surge velocity $v_{\mathrm{th}} \ge 1.2\text{ m/s}$).

sections.heading: Testing in VRX and PX4 SITL: hybrid missions in rough waters
sections.summary: PX4 SITL simulations were conducted using Gazebo Garden and the Virtual RobotX (VRX) environment. Tracking an 8-waypoint boustrophedon path was evaluated in both calm water and a Gerstner wave environment with 1.5 m wave amplitude, confirming stable navigation with tracking errors within vehicle length even in rough seas.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Simulation setup and parameter tuning
Evaluations ran on an Ubuntu 22.04 PC powered by an Intel Core i7 processor and 32 GB RAM, coupling Gazebo Garden v7.9.0 with the Virtual RobotX (VRX) marine simulator. PX4 firmware ran in Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) mode, executing identical binary logic to real hardware. The buoyancy model incorporates a mass-spring-damper system to account for hydrodynamic damping when the drone contacts the water, preventing unwanted resonance.

Vehicle parameters were mass $m = 20\text{ kg}$, pontoon length $L = 1\text{ m}$, pontoon separation $D = 0.6\text{ m}$, and maximum thruster force $T_{\max} = 5\text{ N}$. Control parameters tuned empirically included hand-position distance $l = 1.7\text{ m}$, nominal progression speed $\dot{s}_{\mathrm{nom}} = 5\text{ m/s}$, and waypoint acceptance radius $d_r = 0.5\text{ m}$.

### 5.2 Case 1: Autonomous navigation in calm water
A hybrid mission was executed: taking off from land, flying to the water, landing, navigating an 8-waypoint boustrophedon survey pattern, and returning to the starting point. Along straight segments, path-tracking error remained very low. While transient error spikes occurred during turns, maximum tracking error stayed below the vehicle length (1 m). Thrusters decelerated before reaching waypoints and delivered strong yaw torque to rapidly reorient along the next segment.

### 5.3 Case 2: Wavy conditions (4 s period, 1.5 m significant wave height)
The same mission was executed under severe sea conditions with a 4 s wave period and composite Gerstner waves from two directions producing a 1.5 m significant wave height. Thruster commands exhibited oscillations due to wave dynamics, and straight-line tracking errors rose slightly compared to calm water, but accuracy remained well below vehicle length (1 m). During turns, hydrodynamic forces combined with inertia occasionally pushed error beyond vehicle length, but the controller recovered promptly on the subsequent straight segment, completing the entire mission without failure.

sections.heading: Promising results and hurdles toward practical deployment
sections.summary: Rapid mode transitions and emergency manual overrides worked as designed within the single firmware architecture. At the same time, practical deployment will require additions such as battery-aware mission feasibility checks, smoother path planning, and improved manual steering assistance.
sections.details:
Simulation results proved that the proposed firmware correctly oversees all stages of a hybrid mission, preserving path tracking without saturating control inputs even under wave disturbances. Mode switching via the RC safety switch was very smooth, ensuring operators can regain manual control at any moment.

However, several limitations and challenges were identified:
- **Mission feasibility assessment**: A battery consumption model is not yet integrated, leaving dynamic return-to-launch (RTL) decisions and pre-flight feasibility checks based on remaining capacity unimplemented.
- **Path planning smoothing**: Waypoints are currently linked by simple straight lines, causing discontinuous maneuvers where the vehicle must decelerate and pivot at corners. Introducing a curvature-aware path manager could further suppress turning error spikes.
- **Manual steering assistance**: The current manual mode relies on pure feedforward control, making it sensitive to wind and waves and demanding pilot skill for precise maneuvers. Future work will require assistive features combining velocity feedback and attitude stabilization.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook: real-world validation and further extensions
sections.summary: An extended PX4 firmware that autonomously executes hybrid aerial-marine missions while preserving standard interfaces was developed and validated in simulation. Future plans include porting to physical hardware, conducting waterborne field tests, and implementing dynamic path replanning.
sections.details:
This study presented a novel control framework extending standard PX4 firmware for hybrid unmanned aerial-aquatic vehicles (UAAVs) performing both flight and surface navigation on a single craft. Coordination between the newly created marine navigation module and Navigator ensures high safety for operators and the environment while enabling seamless autonomous operations linked with QGroundControl.

Future work includes porting the firmware onto a physical UAAV platform and conducting field trials on real water bodies. Adding online mission replanning, energy-aware failsafe mechanisms, and advanced marine task directives (such as station keeping for point sampling) will help deliver a practical system ready for aquatic infrastructure inspection and environmental monitoring.

takeaways: Integrating altitude thresholds into PX4's Navigator logic enables natural sequencing of flight, landing, surface navigation, and takeoff solely through waypoint altitude differences in GCS mission files
Even on an underactuated twin-thruster hull, combining the hand-position method with error-adaptive progression slowdown effectively prevents error divergence during sharp turns
Online learning of current disturbances is significantly more robust when gated to update only when ground velocity and path heading align, skipping turning transients
Properly using PX4 standard uORB communication and mode ID management allows entirely different domain control pipelines to coexist without breaking the existing flight codebase
limitations: Validation is limited to Gazebo/VRX SITL simulations; physical phenomena such as severe water spray and hydrodynamic drag during surface touchdown and liftoff remain unverified on hardware
Waypoints are connected by straight lines, requiring deceleration and stopping at turns, which leaves room for improvement in energy efficiency and tracking errors
Mission feasibility checks and autonomous return-to-launch decisions considering remaining battery capacity or power consumption are not yet incorporated
Because manual marine mode uses pure feedforward control, precise vessel handling under environmental disturbances requires experienced pilot skills
